title: Clear out your read-later pile with a local agent
summary: Sarvar Nadaf built Unpile, a laptop-only agent that sorts saved articles into keep, skim or drop; on a 14-item demo it kept 5 and silenced 8.
agent_role: The agent reads an exported reading list and predicts which items the user will read. It decides keep, skim or drop with a plain reason for each, then writes a short morning digest. The user supplies their reading history and export.
outcome: Author reports the demo pile of 14 items came down to 5 keepers, 1 maybe and 8 silenced, saving about 5.5 hours of reading. He says he cleared a 1,247-item backlog.
what_they_did: A developer built Unpile, an agent that runs fully offline on a laptop. You point it at an export from Pocket, Instapaper, browser bookmarks or a spreadsheet. One local model learns from your history of what you actually read and rates each saved item. A second local model writes a two-line morning digest of the keepers.
how_it_went: On the demo pile it kept 5 of 14 items, flagged 1 as maybe and silenced 8. The author says this saved 5.5 hours of reading. He reports letting it clear almost all of his 1,247 saved articles. A live demo and the code are public.
worth_knowing: The project's dataset is synthetic, though documented, so results on your own pile may differ. The digest writer is told never to invent an item, and a simple backup writes the digest if the model is unavailable.
prompt: I have a read-later backlog exported as [Pocket/Instapaper/bookmarks/CSV file]. Go through every item and sort it into keep, skim or drop. Base this on how likely I am to actually read it, using [my history of articles I did read, or my stated interests]. Give a one-line reason for each decision. Then write a calm two-line morning digest of only the keepers, and don't invent any items. Show me the full list of drops and wait for my approval before deleting or archiving anything.

curation.rationale: A working, open-source local agent that triages a read-later pile and writes a digest, with a live demo and code. The training data is synthetic and the real-backlog result is lightly evidenced. Daily-life use earns a small boost.
